The Big Story 

Fierce, bipartisan pushback over Hegseth’s plan for a livestream execution

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s plan to livestream a military firing squad execution next month is causing a fierce outcry of opposition from both sides of the aisle.

© AP Photo/Stephanie Scarbrough

The Pentagon on Thursday revealed a surprise plan to livestream the Dec. 3 firing squad execution of the convicted Fort Hood, Texas, shooter, former Army Maj. Nidal Hasan, in what would be the military’s first execution in six decades.

 

The plan immediately drew fierce blowback from both Republican and Democratic lawmakers, former Trump administration officials and even the leading Catholic bishop in the U.S., who have called the idea barbaric and below the country’s dignity and standards.

 

Vice President Vance was the first administration official to hint at some unease with the Pentagon’s decision, telling reporters Friday that he will not be watching the execution should it be livestreamed.

 

Vance also expressed skepticism that the live stream would even take place, saying, “I don’t know that that’s actually going to happen.”

 

Rep. Austin Scott (R-Ga.), posted to X that while he “absolutely” support’s Hasan’s death sentence, live-streaming executions “is what jihadists do. America is better than that.“

 

Sen. John Curtis (R-Utah), warned that a “civilization erodes when it cultivates an appetite for executions as a form of entertainment,” urging Hegseth to reconsider.

 

And Joe Kent, the former head of the National Counterterrorism Center who resigned in March over the Iran war, said streaming Hasan’s execution is “a stain on our morality.”

 

Hasan, a former Army psychiatrist, opened fire at Fort Hood in 2009, killing 13 people. He has never claimed innocence and is set to be put to death on Dec. 3 at 1 p.m. local time at the same military base, according to Hegseth.

 

Read more at thehill.com.

data.title: French NBA star Wembanyama expresses support for student protests
data.description:
French-born San Antonio Spurs star Victor Wembanyama is expressed support for students in his home country who have taken to the streets in the thousands in recent weeks protesting the conditions of their schools.  

“These are systemic inequalities — problems so deep-rooted ⁠that, in fact, I’m glad that high-school students and young people in general are speaking up,” Wembanyama said in a press conference Thursday, according to online translations. 

“I hear them, and I support them, and ‌I hope the people all over there will do the same,” he added. 

Thousands of French students have taken to the streets since the end of September to protest teacher shortages, building conditions and other problems they say run rampant inside their classrooms.  

The protests have sparked worldwide attention as thousands have been arrested and hundreds injured in the demonstrations. Scores of schools have been damaged or burned.

French officials have tried negotiating with students to no avail, and some have called for parents to be held responsible for any violent acts by the students. 

The debate has made its way to the U.S. as Republicans, including President Trump, blame immigration for the scene in France.  

“What’s happening in France is nothing less than out of control mass migration. This isn’t about schools, this is about Islam wanting to take over a once great Country!” Trump said on Truth Social on Tuesday.

data.title: International Criminal Court 'firmly rejects' new US sanctions
data.description:
The International Criminal Court (ICC) strongly pushed back on Friday after the U.S. imposed new sanctions on its financial assets, slamming the move as “an assault on the rule of law.”

ICC President Tomoko Akane said in a video shared to the court’s website that it “firmly rejects” the U.S.’s retaliation, which Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced Friday morning as former ICC judge Navi Pillay was awarded a Nobel Peace Prize. The Trump administration previously sanctioned Akane in August.

Akane called the latest financial penalties an “attack” on the countries that created the ICC and on international legal order. 

“It is an attack on the victims of mass atrocities who have waited years, sometimes decades, for those to be held to account,” she said.

The international judicial body, based in The Hague, Netherlands, was created in 2002 to address global atrocities when countries are unable or fail to intervene.

The ICC has pursued war crimes cases against U.S.-allied Israel over its military offensive in Gaza. Pillay, who received Nobel recognition for her contributions to boosting the impact of international law, recently oversaw a United Nations report that concluded that Israeli forces committed genocide in the region.

In a video shared on social media announcing these sanctions, Rubio cited the court’s efforts to prosecute American citizens, despite the U.S. not being a member of the ICC. 

“We will ban transactions with this rogue court, cutting off their resources and crippling their ability to operate against us,” Rubio said. “Because our message is clear: the United States and the American people are not subject to the jurisdiction of this fake ICC.”

Rubio also called on U.S. allies who are members of the ICC to “rein in this rogue court.”

Akane said that global leadership must now choose between “a world where might is right” or “a future based on the rule of law.”

“In the face of such attacks, we cannot remain indifferent. All of us, including state parties, have a legal and moral duty to act in defense of the international order,” the judge said. “To stand up for law, not force. We will be judged by history for the choices we make today. 

“I pledge to you: The International Criminal Court will continue its work undeterred, with the firm resolve that justice must prevail,” she continued. 

United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights Volker Türk also denounced the Trump administration’s sanctions on the ICC as “unacceptable” and called for U.S. to withdraw them in a statement his office released Friday. 

“It is abundantly clear in all the conflicts and crises that plague our world that impunity fuels violence and suffering,” Türk said. “We need to be investing more in ensuring justice and accountability – rather than penalizing those who are documenting, investigating and prosecuting serious violations.”

data.title: Trump confirms he will no longer attend Alabama-Georgia game amid Hurricane Isaias
data.description:
President Trump confirmed that he will no longer attend the University of Georgia vs. University of Alabama game in Tuscaloosa on Saturday as Hurricane Isaias barrels toward the Gulf Coast. 

“Based on the fact that a huge Hurricane/Storm is coming, it is important to have our wonderful First Responders, Law Enforcement, and others, focused on that Storm, and in no way be thinking about the safety, or presence, of the President of the United States, ME!” Trump wrote in a Truth Social post. 

The president added that he hopes the game will go on despite the weather, noting that he will be visiting both teams “at a later date.”

Tuscaloosa is not currently projected to be in the eye of the storm but is under a tropical storm warning. 

The game would have been the second Southeastern Conference (SEC) football game Trump has been to this month. Last month, Trump traveled to Knoxville, Tenn. for the Texas-Tennessee game. 

Trump noted in his post that he is still slated to travel to Clarksville, Tenn. for a rally on Saturday. 

“I will go to Tennessee, where we have quickly called a Big Rally in order to get our fantastic Congressional Candidates, our Great Senator, Bill Hagerty, and a woman who will go down as one of the most impactful Governors in the State’s History, Marsha Blackburn, elected!” Trump said.

data.title: Jackson holds slight lead over Collins in Maine Senate race survey
data.description:
Sen. Susan Collins (R-Maine) trails Democratic challenger Troy Jackson in her bid for a sixth term, with less than a month until the midterm elections.

A new Washington Post-Schar School poll found Jackson, a former Maine Senate president, leading Collins 50 percent to 46 percent among Maine voters.

The closely watched contest could play a major role in determining control of the Senate, where Republicans hold a 53-seat majority. Collins is the only Republican senator seeking reelection this year in a state that backed former Vice President Kamala Harris in the 2024 presidential election.

Jackson secured the Democratic nomination after Graham Platner withdrew from the race in July following numerous scandals, including sexual assault allegations, which he denied.

The survey, which was conducted from Sept. 30 to Oct. 5, points to challenges for the Republican as she seeks to distance herself from President Trump, whose approval rating stands at just 36 percent among Maine voters.

Fifty-eight percent of respondents believed Collins was too supportive of Trump in the Senate and 51 percent viewed the five-term incumbent unfavorably. Meanwhile, 43 percent held an unfavorable view of Jackson.

Collins, who chairs the Senate Appropriations Committee, has emphasized her ability to secure federal funding for Maine and work across party lines in an effort to attract independent voters. 

Voters gave the 30-year Senate veteran a 24-point advantage over Jackson on bringing federal dollars to the state and also preferred her approach to bipartisanship.

“To be effective in the Senate, you need knowledge, experience, seniority and relationships,” Collins said during a debate with Jackson. “That combination has allowed me to pass bipartisan legislation.”

Jackson, meanwhile, held an advantage on several issues important to voters, including the economy, health care, abortion and government corruption.

Affordability emerged as the leading concern among Maine voters, with 63 percent describing home energy and utility costs as unaffordable and 62 percent saying the same about gasoline prices amid the Iran war. More than half also said groceries and health care were unaffordable.

Collins has sought to portray Jackson, who has the backing of Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.), as too liberal for Maine, pointing to his support for Medicare for All while simultaneously calling out his previous opposition to abortion rights during his legislative career.

data.title: Live updates: Trump makes deal with Putin for diesel; Vance rallies voters in Ohio with Husted
data.description:
President Trump on Friday announced Russia will supply the U.S. and global market with diesel amid soaring fuel prices.

“I have just concluded a highly successful discussion with President Vladimir Putin, of Russia, wherein it was agreed that Russia will immediately supply over 300,000 Tons of Diesel Fuel to the American and Global Marketplace, another 500,000 Tons during the month of November, and 1,000,000 Tons immediately thereafter,” Trump wrote in a post on Truth Social.

Meanwhile, Trump set in motion an administrative panel Friday to investigate mortgage fraud allegations against Federal Reserve board of governors member Lisa Cook in his latest effort to fire her. The inquiry will include a hearing at the White House on Nov. 5 that Cook “shall” attend to answer questions from the committee, Trump said in a written memo.

Trump marked Columbus Day with an event Friday in the East Room.

Later, he is holding a rally in upstate New York after focusing his crunch-time campaign blitz for GOP candidates in red states.

He will stump in Syracuse, N.Y., to give a last-minute boost to Republican gubernatorial candidate Bruce Blakeman — whom nonpartisan election forecaster Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ) gave a 10 percent chance of winning as of Thursday night.

Within the past week, the president has made stops in Texas, Oklahoma, Alabama and Nebraska — all of which he claimed in 2024. This weekend, he’ll be in Tennessee and Alabama, with a rally in Alaska next week.

Vice President Vance is rallying voters in Lima, Ohio. While DDHQ ranks Ohio’s 4th Congressional District, home to Lima, a “safe” Republican victory, the state’s Senate race is much tighter — with former Sen. Sherrod Brown (D) narrowly leading his GOP opponent, incumbent Sen. Jon Husted (R) as of late September.

Follow live below.

data.title: Kelly calls to remove Hegseth 'immediately' over public execution plan
data.description:
Sen. Mark Kelly (D-Ariz.) called on the Trump administration to remove Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth from his post “immediately” over the Pentagon chief’s plan to livestream the military execution of former Army Maj. Nidal Hasan, the convicted Fort Hood shooter.

Kelly argued the government publicizing Hasan’s death by firing squad is akin to U.S. adversaries’ public execution practices, namely those of Iran and the Taliban. He went on to say the administration should be “delivering for the American people,” not “glorifying violence.”

Hasan was convicted of killing 13 people on a Texas military base in 2009. He is set to be put to death on Dec. 3 — the first military execution in over 60 years.

“There is no doubt that Nidal Hasan is a murderer who took the lives of 13 people and injured dozens. He should face justice for that. But a public execution? Here in the United States?” Kelly wrote in a Friday post to social media platform X. 

Kelly — who has called for Hegseth’s resignation before — said the livestream plan, along with the Pentagon chief’s “maximum lethality” campaign, further justified his removal.

The Arizona Democrat, a retired Navy captain, is suing the Pentagon for censuring him and moving to lower his retirement rank over his participation in a video that reminded troops they must refuse illegal orders. Defense officials argued Kelly was urging service members to defy lawful directives and thus violating military rules, justifying the punishment.

But criticism on the plans for Hasan’s execution reached both sides of the political aisle. Republican Sen. John Curtis (Utah) drew comparisons between Hegseth’s announcement and the fall of the Roman Empire, saying, “A civilization erodes when it cultivates an appetite for executions as a form of entertainment.”

“Secretary Hegseth’s plan to livestream the Fort Hood execution risks feeding that appetite,” Curtis wrote in an X post. “The victims deserve justice administered with solemnity. Broadcasting a death diminishes us and is not an effective deterrent. I urge him to reconsider.”

Another GOP senator, Thom Tillis (N.C.) called the execution plan “beyond disgusting,” while Democratic Sen. Chris Murphy (N.Y.) suggested Hegseth could be mimicking ISIS-style killings. Archbishop Paul Coakley, president of the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops, also weighed in, calling the publicization such capital punishment a “barbaric promotion of a culture of death.”

Kelly concluded his denouncement with a quote from former President Ronald Reagan, a Republican, which he argued exemplifies why public executions do not fit within the U.S.’s character “at our best.”

“As President Ronald Reagan said “compassion, vision, and a fundamental sense of decency are the hallmarks of our national character.” That is not what we’ve seen from this President and his administration,” Kelly said. “We need to find that again.”

data.title: DeSantis withdraws death warrant for first time, calling off execution
data.description:
Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis (R) is withdrawing a death warrant for the first time since he became governor, calling off the execution of 74-year-old William Lee Thompson following the botched execution of Tennessee inmate Christa Pike. 

DeSantis’s letter to Florida State Prison Warden Randall Polk blocks Thompson’s scheduled execution by lethal injection. In the letter, the Florida governor did not outline any reasoning behind his decision.

Thompson’s attorneys previously raised serious concerns about his mental competency and deteriorating physical health, according to the Death Penalty Information Center. Thompson was sentenced to death for his role in the 1976 murder of 23-year-old Sally Ivester.

Thompson was one of two inmates scheduled to be executed on Oct. 13. James Robertson, 63, remains scheduled for execution on Tuesday for the 2008 killing of his cellmate, Frank Hart.

DeSantis’s rare reversal comes after Pike’s failed execution earlier this week where she was injected with two lethal doses of pentobarbital and survived.

The failed execution of Pike, in which she was injected with two lethal doses of pentobarbital and survived, has brought renewed scrutiny to the death penalty nationwide, even in states like Florida that have altered their lethal injection procedure to not include pentobarbital.

Pike’s lawyers report that she is alive and speaking but sustained “severe damage” to her arms and remains handcuffed and shackled to a hospital bed and that she was receiving “lifesaving care” in the hospital.

Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee (R) has ordered that Pike’s execution be delayed until at least next year.

The U.S. military is also scheduling its first execution in decades of convicted Fort Hood shooter Nidal Hasan. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth announced on Thursday the execution would be by firing squad and livestreamed which was criticized by GOP lawmakers – including Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.).

In the past two years, the rate of executions in Florida has increased with 19 in 2025 and 16 in 2026 so far. Previously, the Sunshine State had not executed more than eight inmates in a year, doing so in 1984 and 2014, according to the Florida Department of Corrections. The state currently also leads for the highest number of executions in 2026 so far.

data.title: Southwest Airlines says 'brief' system outage affected boarding, checked bags
data.description:
(NEXSTAR) – Southwest Airlines experienced a “brief” outage on Friday morning that affected the computer systems used to help check baggage and board flights.

Southwest confirmed the news shortly after travelers began to report delays.

“Southwest experienced a brief interruption due to a system outage at our vendor, Amadeus,” a spokesperson for the airline wrote in an emailed statement to Nexstar. “The airline continued to check baggage and board flights manually while full functionality was restored.”

The Amadeus IT Group, referenced in the statement, is a provider of travel software utilized by numerous global airlines.

“Amadeus briefly experienced a technical issue today affecting Southwest Airlines, originating from a third-party technology provider,” the IT company wrote. “Our teams took immediate action and worked closely with the provider to restore normal operations. We apologize for any inconvenience caused.”

Outage-detection platform DownDetector showed that passengers began reporting issues with Southwest shortly before 9 a.m., EDT on Friday.

Travelers claimed on social media that their gate agents were unable to scan their boarding passes, or that workers at the check-in gate were issuing handwritten baggage tickets. Others said they were told that all flights had been halted amid the outage, though the airline has disputed that was the case.

“[Flights were] not halted, just slowed due to manual processes,” a Southwest spokesperson said.

The airline’s initial statement also apologized to affected passengers.

We apologize to our Customers for any inconvenience and working to get them to their destinations as quickly as possible,” a spokesperson wrote. “Nothing is more important to Southwest than the Safety of our Customers and Employees.”

data.title: Trump: Russia will supply US with diesel
data.description:
Russia will supply the U.S. with diesel, President Trump announced on Friday.

“I have just concluded a highly successful discussion with President Vladimir Putin, of Russia, wherein it was agreed that Russia will immediately supply over 300,000 Tons of Diesel Fuel to the American and Global Marketplace, another 500,000 Tons during the month of November, and 1,000,000 Tons immediately thereafter,” Trump wrote in a post on Truth Social.

“Additionally, based on the condition of their Diesel Refineries, Russia will then deliver, within a short period of time, 3,000,000 Tons of Diesel Fuel,” he added. 

The announcement comes as high diesel prices, tied in part to the Iran conflict, have contributed to inflation and have particularly presented issues for farmers. The matter has become a major midterm issue.

Developing.
